name: Neutron
info: An atomic nucleus, or a [em1]nuclide[em1], is made of [em2]protons[em2] and [em3]neutrons[em3]. Protons have a positive charge to counteract the negative charge of [em2]electrons[em2] that orbit in shells around the nucleus. Neutrons have [em3]zero[em3] [em3]charge[em3]; that is to say they are neutral.[br] [br]More neutrons in a nucleus do not change an element's chemical properties but they do make it [em1]heavier[em1] and they can affect how [em2]stable[em2] the nuclide is. Nuclides that are not stable [em2]decay[em2] into other nuclides. The measure for how long a given nuclide will last is called its [em3]half-life[em3]. Nuclides decay [em1]at random[em1] so it's impossible to know exactly when a particular nuclide will decay. Instead, how long it takes about half of a bunch of the same nuclide to decay is measurable, and that's what half-life means.[br] [br]The nuclide that is a lone free neutron, [link]Neutron-1[link], has a half-life of about 10 minutes. This means if you had 1000 free neutrons then after ten minutes you could expect to have only 500, and only 250 left after 20 minutes. Neutrons can be stable when combined with protons inside an [em1]atomic nucleus[em1].

name: Hydrogen
info: As the very first element [em3]Hydrogen[em3] has only one proton. It's not just first on the Periodic Table, though, it's literally [em1]the first element to exist[em1]. To this day [em2]75% of all the matter in the universe is Hydrogen[em2].[br] [br]Hydrogen on its own is usually a [em1]gas[em1]. The two H's in [em3]H[sub]2[sub]O[em3] are the two Hydrogen atoms, combined with one Oxygen atom, to make [em2]water[em2]. In many common reactions between [em1]acids (like vinegar - C[sub]2[sub]H[sub]4[sub]O[sub]2[sub])[em1] and [em2]bases[em2] [em2](like baking soda - NaHCO[sub]3[sub])[em2], the acid gives a Hydrogen to the base.[br] [br]Hydrogen has two stable isotopes: [link]Hydrogen-1[link] with zero neutrons, also called [em3]Protium[em3], and [link]Hydrogen-2[link] with one neutron, also called [em3]Deuterium[em3] (remember: the number comes from the sum of neutrons and protons). With two neutrons, [link]Hydrogen-3[link] also has a special name: [em3]Tritium[em3]. Tritium has a [em1]half-life[em1] of 12.32 years, making it the most stable [em1]radioisotope[em1] of Hydrogen (isotopes that are [em2]radioactive[em2] and decay). All the other isotopes of Hydrogen are very unstable and have half-lives that are only fractions of a second.

name: Helium
info: [em3]Helium[em3] is the lightest [em2]noble gas[em2], meaning it is both incredibly light and very non-reactive. In fact, to make [em1]compounds[em1] with Helium and other elements, it usually requires extreme temperatures or pressures.[br] [br]While Helium is the [em2]second most abundant[em2] element in the universe after [link]Hydrogen[link] it is somewhat rare on Earth because it is so light and non-reactive that it tends to float up to the top of the atmosphere and [em2]escape to space[em2]. Helium also has the lowest [em1]boiling point[em1] of any element, meaning its liquid state is incredibly cold [em2](around 4.2 K, or ​−452° F / −269° C)[em2]. This makes liquid Helium ideal for applications that require extremely low temperatures, such as the [em3]superconducting magnets[em3] used in MRI machines, particle accelerators, and quantum computers.[br] [br]When an atomic nucleus decays by [em3]Alpha (α) decay[em3] it emits an Alpha particle, composed of two [em1]neutrons and two protons[em1]... the same thing as a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus. This reduces the parent nucleus's atomic number by two, for example turning [link]Uranium-238[link] into [link]Thorium-234[link] + [link]Helium-4[link].

name: Boron
info: [em3]Boron[em3] has five protons and isn't made by [em1]fusion inside stars[em1]. Instead it comes from [em1]cosmic ray spallation[em1], where high-energy cosmic rays break apart heavier nuclei, and from supernovas. It's rare in the solar system and makes up only about [em2]0.001% of Earth's crust by weight[em2].[br] [br]Boron has two stable isotopes: [link]Boron-11[link] (about 80% of natural boron) and [link]Boron-10[link] (about 20%). Boron-10 has a high [em2]cross-section for neutron capture[em2], meaning it's very good at [em3]absorbing neutrons[em3]. That makes boron useful in nuclear reactors, in control rods and boric acid, for fission control and emergency shutdown.[br] [br]The same property is used in medicine. In [em1]boron neutron capture therapy[em1], a Boron-10 compound is taken up by a tumor and hit with low-energy neutrons. Each capture releases an alpha particle (a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus) and a [link]Lithium-7[link] ion, which travel only a short distance, so the damage stays close to the tumor cells.[br] [br]Boron-11 is also a candidate fuel for [em1]aneutronic fusion[em1], a kind of fusion that produces few neutrons. Hit by a proton of about 500 keV, it produces [em3]three alpha particles[em3] and [em3]8.7 MeV of energy[em3].

name: Nitrogen
info: [em3]Nitrogen[em3] is one of the most common elements in the universe. Two atoms of it bond to form diatomic Nitrogen gas (N[sub]2[sub]), which makes up [em2]78% of Earth's atmosphere[em2].[br] [br]Nitrogen occurs in all organisms, primarily in [em1]amino acids[em1] (and thus proteins), in the [em1]nucleic acids (DNA and RNA)[em1] and in the energy transfer molecule [em1]adenosine triphosphate (ATP)[em1] that powers all cells. The human body contains about 3% nitrogen by mass. Because of its importance for life Nitrogen is a key component of [em2]fertilizers[em2], usually in the form of [em2]Ammonia (NH[sub]3[sub])[em2].[br] [br]Nitrogen has many industrial applications. Due to its abundance, [em3]low boiling point (−195°C / −320°F)[em3], and low rate of evaporative loss [em3]liquid nitrogen[em3] is commonly used for cooling things to very low temperatures. This can include [em2]cryotherapies[em2] such as removing skin cysts and warts, [em2]cryopreservation[em2] of biological materials, and cooling sensitive electronics such as [em2]infrared and x-ray detectors[em2].

name: Scandium
info: [em3]Scandium[em3] has 21 protons and one stable isotope, [link]Scandium-45[link], so all natural scandium is the same nuclide. It was made in [em1]supernova explosions[em1] and by cosmic rays breaking apart heavier nuclei. It's about as common in Earth's crust as [link]Cobalt[link], but it's rarely concentrated and mostly comes as a [em2]byproduct of mining[em2].[br] [br]The world makes only a [em2]few dozen metric tons[em2] of scandium a year, but it's put to good use. Adding just a little to [link]Aluminium[link] makes a [em1]stronger alloy[em1] that has been used in Russian MiG fighter jets, baseball bats, bicycle frames, and lacrosse sticks. Scandium is also used in [em3]metal-halide lamps[em3], which make a white light close enough to sunlight for TV cameras to capture good color.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Scandium-46[link], with a half-life of about 84 days, is used as a [em1]tracer in oil refineries[em1]. [link]Scandium-45[link] is even being studied for a [em2]nuclear clock[em2] that could, in theory, be far more precise than [link]Caesium[link] clocks.[br] [br]Scandium was found in 1879 by Swedish chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson, and is named after [em3]Scandinavia[em3].

name: Vanadium
info: [em3]Vanadium[em3] has 23 protons, and nearly all natural vanadium (over 99%) is [link]Vanadium-51[link]. The other small percentage is [link]Vanadium-50[link], which is technically radioactive but has a half-life of about 270 quadrillion years, so it's [em1]effectively stable[em1].[br] [br]Vanadium has a moderate neutron-capture cross-section, and the isotopes it forms under neutron exposure have short half-lives, so it's considered a suitable material for the [em2]inner structure of a fusion reactor[em2].[br] [br]About 85% of Vanadium is used as an additive that [em2]significantly increases the strength of steel[em2]. The first large-scale industrial use was in the chassis of the [em1]Ford Model T[em1], and Vanadium steel is also used in axles, bicycle frames, crankshafts, and gears. It strengthens [link]Titanium[link] alloys for jet engines too, and [em3]Vanadium redox batteries[em3] are used for grid energy storage.[br] [br]It was named for Vanadís, another name for the [em3]Norse goddess Freyja[em3], because of its colorful compounds. Sea squirts are known to concentrate Vanadium in their blood cells.

name: Iron
info: [em3]Iron[em3] is a widely used metal that's the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. Extracting usable metal from ores containing Iron requires kilns or furnaces capable of reaching 1,500°C (2,730°F), about 500°C (900°F) higher than that required to smelt [link]Copper[link]. Humans first developed this technology around 4,000 years ago, leading to the [em2]Iron Age[em2].[br] [br]Iron is the [em1]heaviest element created by stellar fusion[em1]. Inside the core of stars fusing lighter elements to make heavier ones releases net energy, but Iron is the first element that when fused consumes energy. All elements heavier than Iron are either produced in [em3]supernova explosions[em3] or by means other than stellar fusion.[br] [br]Iron regularly forms various compounds with [link]Oxygen[link]. When metals [em1]rust[em1] it is the Iron combining with Oxygen to form [em3]Iron(III) Oxide (Fe[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3]. The same affinity for Oxygen is why human blood is red; Iron in [em2]Hemoglobin[em2] is how red blood cells hold Oxygen for delivery to cells all around the body.

name: Germanium
info: [em3]Germanium[em3] is one of the [em2]purest materials ever made[em2]: zone refining leaves about one impurity atom in 10 billion. Like water, Germanium [em1]expands when it freezes[em1]. Pure crystals can even grow metal 'whiskers' that shorted out early transistors.[br] [br]The first [em2]transistors[em2], built in 1947, were made of Germanium, which was the [em3]basis of all semiconductor electronics[em3] until the early 1970s when [link]Silicon[link] took over. Germanium transistors powered early [em1]guitar fuzz pedals[em1], and some audio circuits still prefer Germanium diodes for their smoother clipping.[br] [br]Today most Germanium goes into [em1]fiber optic cables[em1], infrared lenses for thermal cameras, and a catalyst for making PET plastic. Germanium also underlies Mars rover solar cells, and ultra-pure crystals detect gamma rays in [em2]searches for dark matter[em2].[br] [br]Germanium supplements were once sold as cancer treatments, but there is no evidence they work, and long-term users of one injectable form developed [em1]kidney damage[em1].

name: Bromine
info: [em3]Bromine[em3] is one of only two elements that are [em1]liquid at room temperature[em1], along with [link]Mercury[link]. This reddish-brown liquid boils at just 59°C and gives off a [em3]harsh choking vapor[em3]. Frozen at -195°C it's pale yellow, and squeezed to 55 gigapascals it becomes a [em2]metal[em2].[br] [br][em2]Seawater is about 65 parts per million Bromine[em2], and the Dead Sea is rich enough to be a major source. The oceans release an estimated 1 to 2 million tons of bromoform a year, and organic Bromine compounds are [em1]the most common organohalides in nature[em1].[br] [br]Your own immune cells use it: eosinophils [em3]prefer bromide to chloride[em3] when killing parasites. Potassium bromide was the [em1]only effective epilepsy drug[em1] until 1912, but large doses cause 'bromism' sickness.[br] [br]More than half of all Bromine goes into [em2]flame retardants[em2]. It was also added to leaded gasoline, and as brominated vegetable oil to citrus sodas, until the [em3]US banned it in food in 2024[em3]. Bromine atoms high in the atmosphere [em1]destroy ozone[em1], which has led to restrictions on methyl bromide.

name: Rubidium
info: [em3]Rubidium[em3] is a very soft silvery metal that melts at just 39°C. It's the first alkali metal [em1]denser than water[em1], and it [em2]reacts explosively[em2] with it. Its flame is nearly the same purple as [link]Potassium[link]'s, so telling them apart takes a spectroscope. Rubidium silver iodide has the [em1]highest room-temperature conductivity of any ionic crystal[em1].[br] [br]In 1995, cooling [link]Rubidium-87[link] atoms close to absolute zero created a [em2]Bose-Einstein condensate[em2], a Nobel Prize-winning state of matter. Rubidium is also used in [em1]atomic clocks[em1] for telecom equipment and satellite navigation. Rubidium-87 is radioactive and decays into [link]Strontium-87[link], so geologists use the ratio to [em3]date rocks[em3].[br] [br]The synthetic [link]Rubidium-82[link] lasts only about 76 seconds, yet it's used in [em3]PET scans[em3] of the heart and of brain tumors, since Rubidium builds up in tumor tissue.[br] [br]Rubidium behaves like [link]Potassium[link] in the body, and a 70 kg person holds about 0.36 grams of it. Only 2 to 4 tons of Rubidium compounds are produced each year, mostly from the mineral [em2]lepidolite[em2].

name: Rhodium
info: [em3]Rhodium[em3] has 45 protons and only one stable isotope, [link]Rhodium-103[link], which makes up 100% of natural Rhodium. It's one of the [em1]rarest elements in Earth's crust[em1] with less than one part per billion. The world produces only about 30 metric tons a year, mostly in South Africa.[br] [br]About 80% of it goes into [em1]catalytic converters[em1], where Rhodium helps [em2]reduce nitrogen oxide emissions[em2]. Its price has swung from under $700 per troy ounce in 2016 to nearly $30,000 in 2021.[br] [br]Rhodium also has a job in nuclear power. [em2]Rhodium neutron detectors[em2] measure neutron flux levels in reactors, and each of the three reactors at Palo Verde has over 300 of them to give a [em2]3D picture of reactivity[em2]. Rhodium is also a [em1]fission product[em1] of [link]Uranium-235[link], but recovering it from used fuel is complex and expensive.[br] [br]Rhodium is [em3]electroplated[em3] onto white [link]Gold[link] and [link]Platinum[link] jewelry for a reflective finish. It was discovered in 1803 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston and named from the Greek [em3]rhodon[em3], 'rose', for the color of one of its compounds.

name: Palladium
info: [em3]Palladium[em3] absorbs [link]Hydrogen[link] at room temperature, so membranes of it make high-purity hydrogen, and it was a key part of the controversial late-1980s [em2]cold fusion[em2] experiments.[br] [br]The biggest use of Palladium by far is [em1]catalytic converters[em1]. It's also used for [em3]electrodes in ceramic capacitors[em3], in pacemakers, spark plugs, and blood sugar test strips, and, since 1939, in white gold jewelry as an alternative to [link]Platinum[link]. Palladium chloride turns carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide, which makes it useful in CO detectors.[br] [br]Palladium chloride was once prescribed for [em2]tuberculosis[em2]. During World War II, when Platinum was a strategic resource, many jewelry bands were made of Palladium, and the Soviet Union minted a [em1]25-ruble Palladium coin[em1]. In 2001 Ford stockpiled Palladium and [em2]lost nearly a billion dollars[em2] when prices fell.[br] [br]People allergic to Palladium often react to [link]Nickel[link] too. English chemist William Hyde Wollaston identified it in 1802 and [em1]named it after the asteroid Pallas[em1].

name: Cadmium
info: [em3]Cadmium[em3] is unusually resistant to corrosion, so some of it goes into [em2]plating aircraft steel[em2]. In 2009, 86% went into [em3]batteries[em3], mostly rechargeable nickel-cadmium cells. Cadmium compounds make [em1]red, orange, and yellow pigments[em1], Cadmium telluride makes solar cells, and Cadmium in reactor control rods [em2]absorbs neutrons[em2].[br] [br][em1]Cadmium is toxic.[em1] Japan's itai-itai disease was linked to Cadmium-contaminated rice. Its biological half-life in humans is 20 to 40 years, and smokers have 4 to 5 times the blood Cadmium of non-smokers. In 2022 Consumer Reports found it in [em3]all 28 dark chocolates[em3] it tested.[br] [br]It's about 650 times scarcer than [link]Zinc[link] in Earth's crust and mostly a by-product of Zinc production. Phosphate fertilizers carry it into crops, while willow and poplar trees can pull it from soil. Cadmium-plated tools were [em2]banned from the U-2 and SR-71 programs[em2] for contaminating [link]Titanium[link], and the EU's RoHS directive now bans it in electronics.

name: Indium
info: [em3]Indium[em3] is so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and bending it makes a [em1]high-pitched cry[em1]. It melts at just 157°C, and it dissolves in liquid [link]Mercury[link] at over 50% by mass, more than any other metal.[br] [br]Indium's biggest use is Indium tin oxide, a transparent [em3]conductive coating on glass for flat-panel displays[em3]. LCD monitors and TVs account for about half of Indium use. Indium compounds also make [em1]LEDs, laser diodes[em1], and thin-film solar cells. Alloys that melt between 50 and 100°C trigger fire sprinklers, and Galinstan, a [link]Gallium[link]-Indium-[link]Tin[link] alloy, replaces Mercury in some thermometers.[br] [br]In World War II, Indium coated bearings in [em1]high-performance aircraft engines[em1]. It's also in [em2]YInMn Blue[em2], the first new inorganic blue pigment in about 200 years.[br] [br]Indium is about as rare in Earth's crust as [link]Silver[link] and is produced only as a by-product of other metals, mostly [link]Zinc[link]. [em3]Less than 1% is recycled.[em3] It has no known biological role and is toxic when inhaled or injected, but poorly absorbed when swallowed.

name: Antimony
info: [em3]Antimony[em3] is a brittle silvery metalloid. Its pentafluoride is the key ingredient of [em2]fluoroantimonic acid[em2], a superacid, and its hydride, stibine, falls apart at room temperature. Antimony also goes into [link]Indium[link] antimonide infrared detectors and [em1]phase-change memory[em1].[br] [br]About half of the world's Antimony goes into [em2]flame retardants[em2], and a third into [em3]lead-acid batteries[em3]. It also [em1]hardens [link]Lead[link][em1] in sailboat keels, bullets, solder, type metal, and pewter, clears bubbles from glass, and steadies friction in brake pads.[br] [br]Antimony's sulfide mineral, [em3]stibnite[em3], was used as the eye cosmetic 'kohl' in predynastic Egypt as early as about [em1]3100 BCE[em1], and its symbol Sb comes from the Latin [em3]stibium[em3]. Doctors once prescribed an [em2]Antimony pill[em2] that could be swallowed, passed, and used again.[br] [br]Antimony and many of its compounds are toxic, like its [em2]group 15[em2] companion [link]Arsenic[link], but far less so. It can leach from PET plastic bottles into drinks.

name: Tellurium
info: [em3]Tellurium[em3] has 52 protons and eight naturally occurring isotopes. Six are stable, and two, [link]Tellurium-128[link] and [link]Tellurium-130[link], are radioactive with extremely long half-lives. Tellurium-128 has [em1]the longest known half-life of any radionuclide[em1]: trillions of trillions of years.[br] [br]Tellurium is [em2]far more common in the universe than on Earth[em2], where its abundance in the crust (~1 part per billion) is comparable to [link]Platinum[link]. Astronomers have seen Tellurium [em2]produced in neutron star mergers[em2].[br] [br]In 2022 about 40% of Tellurium went into [em1]solar panels[em1] made with [link]Cadmium[link] telluride (CdTe), and about 30% into thermoelectric devices. It's also used in [em3]rewritable optical discs and in phase-change memory chips[em3]. Bombarding it with neutrons is the most common way to make [link]Iodine-131[link], which treats some thyroid conditions.[br] [br]Tellurium is mostly a by-product of [link]Copper[link] refining, where 1000 tons of copper ore yields only about one kilogram. Its name comes from the Latin [em3]tellus[em3], meaning 'earth'.

name: Praseodymium
info: [em3]Praseodymium[em3] is a soft silvery rare earth that [em2]tarnishes fast[em2]: a centimeter-sized sample corrodes away completely in about a year. It's mixed in with other rare earths in ores like bastnäsite and monazite, and China produces over 80% of the world's supply.[br] [br]Together with [link]Neodymium[link], Praseodymium makes [em1]powerful permanent magnets[em1] for electric vehicles and wind turbines. Added to [link]Magnesium[link] it strengthens metal for aircraft engines, and a Praseodymium-[link]Nickel[link] compound has a magnetocaloric effect strong enough to [em2]cool to within a thousandth of a degree of absolute zero[em2].[br] [br]Praseodymium tints glass, enamels, and ceramics yellow, and [em1]didymium glass[em1] goggles protect welders and glassblowers. In some crystals it has [em2]slowed a pulse of light to a few hundred meters per second[em2].[br] [br]Some methane-eating bacteria in volcanic mudpots [em3]need rare earths[em3] to live, and Praseodymium works for them about as well as [link]Lanthanum[link] or [link]Cerium[link].

name: Dysprosium
info: [em3]Dysprosium[em3] has 66 protons and [em1]seven stable isotopes[em1], led by [link]Dysprosium-164[link] at about 28% of the natural total. It's also very good at [em2]absorbing neutrons[em2], so mixtures of [em3]Dysprosium Oxide (Dy[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3] and [link]Nickel[link] are used as control rods in nuclear reactors.[br] [br]But dysprosium is best known for its [em1]magnets[em1]. Replacing a bit of the [link]Neodymium[link] in neodymium magnets with dysprosium (up to 6%) helps them keep their magnetism in demanding uses like [em3]electric vehicle motors[em3] and [em3]wind turbine generators[em3]. An electric car can contain up to 100 grams of it.[br] [br]Dysprosium and [link]Holmium[link] have the highest magnetic strengths of any elements, especially at low temperatures. Dysprosium is also in [em2]Terfenol-D[em2], an alloy that changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other known material at room temperature, and is used in [em1]transducers and fuel injectors[em1].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek for [em3]'hard to get'[em3] as its discoverer, French chemist Paul Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, needed more than 30 attempts to separate it.

name: Holmium
info: [em3]Holmium[em3] has the [em1]highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element[em1]. That makes it useful in the [em2]pole pieces of some of the strongest static magnets[em2] ever built.[br] [br]Holmium oxide [em2]changes color with the light[em2]. It looks yellowish in daylight, orange red under some lamps, and pink under others. Its sharp absorption peaks also make Holmium glass a standard for [em1]calibrating laboratory spectrophotometers[em1].[br] [br][em3]Holmium lasers[em3] are used for [em1]kidney stone removal[em1] and prostate surgery. Radioactive [link]Holmium-166[link] is used in targeted liver cancer therapy and as an [em3]MRI contrast agent[em3]. In 2017 IBM stored a bit of data on a [em2]single Holmium atom[em2].[br] [br]Holmium is about as common in Earth's crust as [link]Tungsten[link]. When English physicist Henry Moseley studied atomic numbers, his Holmium sample was so impure that he [em1]gave it the number 66[em1], which really belongs to [link]Dysprosium[link].

name: Erbium
info: [em3]Erbium[em3] plays a key role in [em1]fiber-optic communications[em1]. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers [em2]boost light signals[em2] in the cables.[br] [br]Erbium oxides are used to apply a [em1]pink tint to glass, cubic zirconia, and porcelain[em1]. Erbium(III) chloride can even [em3]glow pink in sunlight[em3].[br] [br]Water absorbs the light of an [em1]Erbium laser[em1] so strongly that it affects only the surface of tissue, leading to uses in [em3]dermatology and dentistry[em3]. An Erbium-[link]Nickel[link] alloy holds unusually large amounts of heat near liquid [link]Helium[link] temperatures, and a little Erbium makes [link]Vanadium[link] softer and easier to work. Erbium also absorbs neutrons, so it serves in [em2]nuclear reactor control rods[em2].[br] [br]Erbium is [em1]never found uncombined in nature[em1], and most of the world's supply comes from clays in southern China. For decades chemists [em2]confused Erbium and[em2] [link]Terbium[link], even swapping their names.

name: Thulium
info: [em3]Thulium[em3] is one of the [em1]rarest of the rare earth metals[em1]. Only radioactive [link]Promethium[link] is scarcer among the Lanthanides. Thulium is [em2]never found pure[em2], and most of it comes from clays in southern China.[br] [br]Put Thulium in a nuclear reactor and neutrons turn some of it into [link]Thulium-170[link], which makes a [em2]portable X-ray source[em2]. This lasts about a year and needs only a small cup of [link]Lead[link] for shielding. It's used in medical and dental X-rays, industrial radiography, and increasingly in [em1]cancer brachytherapy[em1].[br] [br]Thulium glows blue under ultraviolet light, which helps [em3]protect banknotes from counterfeiting[em3]. Thulium lasers remove tissue only at the surface, making them [em1]useful for surgery[em1]. In 2023 researchers proposed Thulium(II) halides for [em2]power-generating windows[em2].[br] [br]Early chemists never saw Thulium's [em3]green color[em3] because their samples were never pure enough. British chemist Charles James needed [em1]15,000 purification operations[em1] to show his material was uniform as the first researcher to obtain a nearly pure sample.

name: Ytterbium
info: [em3]Ytterbium[em3] is unusual among the rare earths. Most form +3 ions, but Ytterbium readily forms +2 ions too, and those are strong enough to [em2]break apart water[em2]. The metal is much less dense than its neighbors [link]Thulium[link] and [link]Lutetium[link], and has [em1]the smallest liquid range of any metal[em1].[br] [br]Ytterbium's electrical resistance rises under high stress, so it's [em2]used to monitor ground movement from earthquakes and explosions[em2]. Powdered Ytterbium can [em1]self-ignite[em1], and mixed with PTFE it burns with an [em3]emerald-green flame[em3].[br] [br]In 2013 NIST built Ytterbium [em1]atomic clocks[em1] from about 10,000 laser-cooled atoms, stable to within less than two parts in 1 quintillion. Ytterbium-doped [em2]fiber lasers[em2] have pushed past 2 kilowatts of power. A single trapped Ytterbium ion could support a clock accurate to 17 decimal places.[br] [br]Ytterbium fluoride makes [em3]dental fillings that slowly release fluoride[em3]. Researchers are also testing Ytterbium oxide in infrared decoy flares.

name: Iridium
info: [em3]Iridium[em3] has 77 protons and two stable isotopes: [link]Iridium-193[link] (about 63% of natural iridium) and [link]Iridium-191[link] (about 37%). It's formed by rapid neutron capture in [em1]neutron star mergers[em1], and it's one of the least abundant elements in Earth's crust, though much more common in meteorites.[br] [br]That rarity is why a thin iridium-rich layer of clay at the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods [em2]66 million years ago[em2] stood out. In 1980 a team led by American physicist Luis Alvarez proposed it came from space, and the idea that a [em3]meteor impact caused the extinction of the dinosaurs[em3] is now widely accepted.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Iridium-192[link], with a half-life of about 74 days, is used in [em1]brachytherapy[em1] (a form of cancer radiotherapy) and industrial radiography. Iridium is the [em3]second-densest[em3] metal after [link]Osmium[link] and the [em3]most corrosion-resistant[em3] metal known, so it's used in spark plug electrodes and in crucibles for growing crystals. It's named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because its compounds have a [em2]variety of colors[em2].

name: Astatine
info: [em3]Astatine[em3] has 85 protons and [em1]no stable isotopes[em1]. The longest-lived, [link]Astatine-210[link], has a half-life of just 8.1 hours. The element's name comes from the [em2]Greek for 'unstable'[em2].[br] [br]That makes it [em3]the rarest naturally occurring element[em3]. Any Astatine present when the Earth formed is long gone, and the little that exists is constantly forming as a decay product of [link]Uranium[link] and [link]Thorium[link]. The entirety of the Earth's crust is estimated to hold [em2]less than one gram[em2] at any given time.[br] [br]Astatine was first produced in 1940 at UC Berkeley by bombarding [link]Bismuth-209[link] with alpha particles ([link]Helium-4[link] nuclei) in a cyclotron. Today [link]Astatine-211[link], with a half-life of 7.2 hours, is being studied for [em1]targeted alpha-particle therapy[em1], though it has to be used quickly.[br] [br]No one has ever seen a solid sample of astatine, because any visible amount would be [em3]vaporized by the heat of its own radioactivity[em3]. It's the heaviest naturally occurring halogen, in the same group as [link]Iodine[link].

name: Francium
info: [em3]Francium[em3] has no stable isotopes, and its longest-lived has a half-life of only 22 minutes. [em1]As little as 28 grams[em1] (1 ounce) exists in Earth's crust at any moment, making it the [em3]second rarest naturally occurring element[em3] after [link]Astatine[link]. Its decay heat would instantly vaporize any visible piece, so nobody has ever seen one.[br] [br]Scientists make Francium by firing [link]Oxygen[link] ions at a [link]Gold[link] target, then hold the atoms in a [em1]laser trap[em1] for about 30 seconds each. One trap held over a million atoms at once. Its simple structure suits precision experiments, including searches for [em2]CP violation[em2], but it has no commercial uses.[br] [br]Francium is the [em2]second most electropositive element[em2], behind [link]Caesium[link], yet its first ionization energy is slightly higher than Caesium's. It should melt around room temperature, and chemists separate it by [em1]coprecipitating it with Caesium salts[em1].[br] [br]French physicist Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 while purifying [link]Actinium[link]. It was the [em3]last element discovered in nature[em3] rather than made in the lab.

name: Radium
info: [em3]Radium[em3] has 88 protons, and all 33 of its known isotopes are [em2]radioactive[em2]. The longest-lived, [link]Radium-226[link], has a half-life of 1600 years and makes up almost all natural Radium. It decays into the gas [link]Radon[link], which is a major source of Radium's danger. Radium makes up roughly [em1]one part per trillion of Earth's crust[em1].[br] [br]French physicists Marie and Pierre Curie discovered Radium in 1898. Its name comes from the Latin [em3]radius[em3] for 'ray'. The radiation makes Radium metal stay warm and [em2]makes nearby chemicals glow[em2], so radium paint was used on watch dials. Dial painters who licked their brushes to a fine point were poisoned, and the [em1]Radium Girls[em1] sued their employer in the 1920s. Radium was also added to soap, cosmetics and drinks for supposed health benefits.[br] [br]The body mistakes Radium for [link]Calcium[link], so it [em1]builds up in bones[em1]. Ironically, that makes [link]Radium-223[link], with a half-life of 11.4 days, a [em2]modern treatment for cancer[em2] that has spread to the bones. The 'curie', the original (and still widely used) unit of radioactivity, was first defined as the activity of one gram of [link]Radium-226[link].

name: Protactinium
info: [em3]Protactinium[em3] has 91 protons and [em1]no stable isotopes[em1]. The longest-lived, [link]Protactinium-231[link], has a half-life of about 33,000 years, and it's found in nature because it is produced by the decay of naturally-occurring [link]Uranium-235[link].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek [em2]protos[em2], meaning 'first', because [link]Protactinium-231[link] decays into [link]Actinium[link].[br] [br]Protactinium also shows up in nuclear energy. In the [em1]thorium fuel cycle[em1], [link]Thorium-232[link] absorbs a neutron and eventually becomes [link]Protactinium-233[link], which decays into [link]Uranium-233[link]. But Protactinium-233 absorbs neutrons too, making it a [em2]neutron poison[em2], so it's removed from thorium reactors as they run.[br] [br]Protactinium is one of the [em1]rarest and most expensive[em1] natural elements, at just a few parts per trillion of the Earth's crust. In 1961, 127 grams of it were extracted from 60 metric tons of waste. It can also be used for [em3]radiometric dating[em3] of geologic sediments up to 175,000 years old.

name: Americium
info: [em3]Americium[em3] is a synthetic element that can be produced by [link]Uranium[link] or [link]Plutonium[link] being [em2]bombarded with neutrons in nuclear reactors[em2]. It was originally discovered as a part of the [em1]Manhattan Project[em1] to build the first atomic bomb.[br] [br][em3]Smoke detectors[em3] work using Americium. About 0.29 micrograms of [em2]Americium Dioxide (AmO[sub]2[sub])[em2] regularly emits alpha particles ([link]Helium-4[link] nuclei) as the Americium decays to [link]Neptunium-237[link]. A detector measures the flow of ions across a gap, and when smoke enters that gap it [em1]absorbs the alpha particles[em1], triggering the alarm.[br] [br]The name of Americium was chosen to refer to the Americas as an analogy to the previously discovered [link]Europium[link], named for Europe, which is the next lighter element in the same [em2]periodic table group[em2].

name: Curium
info: [em3]Curium[em3] is so radioactive that its own [em2]alpha decay[em2] damages its crystal structure, and Curium-242 gives off up to 120 watts of heat per gram. Curium-244 emits so many neutrons and gamma rays that Curium power generators are impractical, but Curium-242 is used to make [link]Plutonium-238[link] for pacemakers and spacecraft.[br] [br][em1]Alpha particle X-ray spectrometers[em1] on Mars rovers, on the Philae comet lander, and on the Surveyor moon probes have used Curium as a radiation source.[br] [br]One metric ton of spent nuclear fuel contains about 20 grams of Curium. Odd-mass isotopes are [em3]highly fissile[em3]: Curium-245 could go critical with as little as 59 grams surrounded by water. Curium [em3]accumulates in bone and liver[em3], where it promotes cancer.[br] [br]American scientists Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, and Albert Ghiorso made it in 1944 at Berkeley as part of the [em1]secret Manhattan Project[em1], and Seaborg first revealed it on the children's radio show [em2]Quiz Kids[em2]. It's named for Marie and Pierre Curie.

name: Berkelium
info: [em3]Berkelium[em3] is hard to make: only neutron bombardment of [link]Uranium[link] or [link]Plutonium[link] in reactors yields weighable amounts. The first sample, 0.6 micrograms in 1958, took [em2]six years of irradiation[em2], and just over a gram of [link]Berkelium-249[link] has been produced at Oak Ridge since 1967, at about $185 per microgram.[br] [br]Berkelium-249 [em3]emits mostly low-energy beta particles[em3], so it's relatively safe to handle, but it decays into [link]Californium-249[link], a strong alpha emitter that heats samples and [em2]damages their crystal structure[em2]. Berkelium mostly turns up at weapons test sites and accident sites like [em1]Chernobyl and Three Mile Island[em1]. Its +3 ions are [em3]green[em3] in most acids, and its +4 ions are yellow to orange.[br] [br]Berkelium has no use outside research, but it mattered in 2009, when a 22-milligram batch of Berkelium-249 was bombarded with [link]Calcium[link] ions at Dubna, Russia, producing the [em1]first six atoms of Tennessine[em1].[br] [br]Discovered at Berkeley in 1949, it's [em2]named for Berkeley, California[em2], in a manner similar to its chemical homologue [link]Terbium[link], which is named for Ytterby, Sweden.

name: Californium
info: [em3]Californium[em3] has 98 protons and is [em1]synthetic[em1]. [link]Californium-252[link] has a half-life of about 2.6 years, and roughly 3% of its decays are [em1]spontaneous fission[em1], making it a powerful neutron source: just one microgram emits about [em2]2.3 million neutrons per second[em2].[br] [br]That makes it useful as a startup neutron source for some nuclear reactors, for inspecting aircraft parts for cracks and corrosion, for finding water and oil layers in wells, and for portable [link]Gold[link] and [link]Silver[link] prospecting. Its neutrons are even used to treat some [em3]cervical and brain cancers[em3] where other radiation therapy is ineffective.[br] [br]Californium is [em1]extremely scarce[em1]. As of 2003 only two sites made [link]Californium-252[link], producing 0.25 grams a year at Oak Ridge and 0.025 grams a year in Russia.[br] [br]Californium was first made in 1950 in Berkeley, California by bombarding [link]Curium-242[link] with alpha particles ([link]Helium-4[link] nuclei), producing only about [em2]5,000 atoms[em2]. It's named after the University of California and the state. Decades later, [link]Californium-249[link] was the target used to make [link]Oganesson[link], the heaviest element made so far.

name: Einsteinium
info: [em3]Einsteinium[em3] has 99 protons and 18 known isotopes, all radioactive. The longest-lived, [link]Einsteinium-252[link], has a half-life of about 472 days. [em2]None occurs naturally on Earth[em2] and any original supply decayed long ago.[br] [br]Einsteinium was discovered in December 1952 in the debris of [em1]Ivy Mike[em1], the first successful hydrogen bomb test, and named after Albert Einstein. Today it's [em3]made by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons[em3] in high-power reactors, mostly the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and only about a milligram a year is produced.[br] [br]Einsteinium is hard to study. Its [em2]radiation damages its own crystal structure[em2], and the heat it gives off (about 1000 watts per gram) makes it [em1]glow blue in the dark[em1]. It also decays into [link]Berkelium[link] and then [link]Californium[link] at roughly 3% per day, so samples quickly become contaminated.[br] [br]It has almost no uses beyond research. In 1955 researchers at Berkeley used it to make the first 17 atoms of [link]Mendelevium[link].

name: Fermium
info: [em3]Fermium[em3] is where a path to heavier elements ends: [em1]neutron capture can't make nuclides above mass number 257[em1], because [link]Fermium-258[link] splits apart by spontaneous fission in just 370 microseconds. This is called the [em1]Fermium Gap[em1].[br] [br]Fermium was first seen in the fallout of the [em3]Ivy Mike hydrogen bomb[em3] test of 1952 and named for physicist Enrico Fermi, though Cold War secrecy delayed publication until 1955. Reactors make only picogram amounts, and from 10 kilograms of debris from a 1969 test researchers recovered just 4 picograms.[br] [br]Its chemistry has been studied only in solution, a few nanograms at a time. Like [link]Ytterbium[link], Fermium can be [em2]reduced from +3 to +2[em2] with [link]Samarium[link](II) chloride, and a Fermium-Ytterbium alloy was used to measure how readily Fermium sublimes. [em3]Pure Fermium metal has never been made[em3], and it has no use outside basic research.

name: Mendelevium
info: [em3]Mendelevium[em3] has been made only in particle accelerators and [em1]one atom at a time[em1]. In 1955 a Berkeley team bombarded [link]Einsteinium[link] with alpha particles and detected [em2]only 17 atoms[em2] of [link]Mendelevium-256[link], the first isotope of any element made that way. Starting with a microgram of Einsteinium, roughly a million atoms can be produced per hour.[br] [br]Mendelevium's [em3]+2 state is stable in water[em3], and its chemistry has been worked out with a handful of atoms, such as eluting just after [link]Fermium[link] from ion-exchange resin. It's predicted to be a metal with a density near 10.3 g/cm³ that melts around 800°C, but [em1]no bulk metal has been made[em1].[br] [br]It's named after [em2]Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table[em2]. During the Cold War, Seaborg needed U.S. government permission to name an element for a Russian, a choice that did not sit well with some American critics. Mendelevium has no uses outside basic research.

name: Nobelium
info: [em3]Nobelium[em3] is the only f-block element for which the [em1]+2 state[em1] is the most stable one in water. [em2]Relativistic effects stabilize its electrons[em2], so it behaves like an alkaline earth metal: in 1974 it eluted between [link]Calcium[link] and [link]Strontium[link] ions. American scientist Glenn Seaborg predicted this in 1949, and experiments confirmed it 19 years later.[br] [br]Nobelium is [em2]made only in particle accelerators[em2]. Bombarding a [link]Californium-249[link] target with [link]Carbon-12[link] ions for ten minutes yields only about 1,200 atoms of [link]Nobelium-255[link], which a stream of [link]Helium[link] gas carries through a thin tube to be dissolved in acid. It has never [em1]been prepared as a visible lump of metal[em1].[br] [br][em3]Nobelium's discovery was messy.[em3] A Stockholm team claimed it in 1957, but their identification was wrong. Berkeley could not confirm it in 1958, and in 1966 a team at Dubna published the first [em1]complete and incontrovertible report[em1]. It's named after Alfred Nobel, inventor of dynamite, and it has no known uses.

name: Lawrencium
info: [em3]Lawrencium[em3] breaks its group's pattern. Its outermost electron sits in a 7p orbital instead of the usual d orbital, one of the [em1]relativistic effects[em1] on superheavy atoms. In 2015 its ionization energy was measured with [link]Lawrencium-256[link], and at 4.96 eV it was the [em2]lowest of any lanthanide or actinide[em2], matching the relativistic prediction.[br] [br][em2]Where it belongs in the periodic table is still debated.[em2] Most authors put it in group 3 with [link]Scandium[link], [link]Yttrium[link], and [link]Lutetium[link], but some end the actinides at [link]Nobelium[link] and call it [em3]the first transition metal of the seventh period[em3]. Attempts to reduce its +3 ions to +2 or +1 in water failed.[br] [br]It's [em3]made by hitting heavy actinides with light ions[em3] such as [link]Boron[link], [link]Oxygen[link], or [link]Neon[link]. It is the [em2]last of the actinides[em2], and it's [em1]named after Ernest Lawrence[em1], inventor of the cyclotron. Berkeley and Dubna both claimed it in the 1960s, and in 1992 IUPAC gave both teams shared credit. It has no uses outside research.

name: Rutherfordium
info: [em3]Rutherfordium[em3] is the first of the [em1]superheavy[em1] elements, and chemists have tested it atom by atom. It forms a [em1]volatile tetrachloride[em1] that's more volatile than [link]Hafnium[link]'s, and in hydrofluoric acid it forms a hexafluoride complex where Hafnium binds seven or eight fluorides.[br] [br]Early calculations suggested [em2]relativistic effects[em2] might make it behave like [link]Lead[link], but it acts like the heavier cousin of Hafnium. Relativity does flip one thing: it loses its 6d electrons first, unlike Hafnium. It's [em3]predicted to be a dense metal[em3], about 17 g/cm³, that melts near 2100°C.[br] [br]Making it is hard. Two nuclei usually stay together only about 10[sup]-20[sup] seconds, and most Rutherfordium isotopes decay mainly by [em1]spontaneous fission[em1]. It's [em2]named after New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford[em2], the father of nuclear physics. It has no uses beyond research.

name: Dubnium
info: [em3]Dubnium[em3] sits in group 5 below [link]Vanadium[link], [link]Niobium[link], and [link]Tantalum[link]. Experiments found it [em1]mostly behaves like Niobium[em1], sometimes like [link]Protactinium[link], and rarely like Tantalum. Its dominant oxidation state is expected to be +5, and it's [em2]predicted to be a dense metal[em2], about 21.6 g/cm³.[br] [br]Dubnium decays by alpha decay or spontaneous fission because the electric repulsion among its many protons [em1]constantly tears at the nucleus[em1], and fission half-lives fall by about 23 orders of magnitude from [link]Uranium[link] to [link]Nobelium[link]. The most stable known, [link]Dubnium-268[link], has a half-life measured in hours, and the predicted [em2]island of stability[em2] may lie further away than first expected.[br] [br]The Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Soviet Union, reported it in 1968, and Berkeley claimed it in 1970. The dispute became part of the [em1]Transfermium Wars[em1]. It was formally [em3]named Dubnium in 1997 after the town of Dubna.[em3]

name: Seaborgium
info: [em3]Seaborgium[em3] is the heavier relative of [link]Tungsten[link] and [link]Molybdenum[link], and chemists have studied it atom by atom. It forms a [em1]volatile oxychloride[em1]. In 2014 the colatile compound [em2]Seaborgium hexacarbonyl Sg(CO)[sub]6[sub][em2] was discovered and found to react readily with [link]Silicon[link] dioxide.[br] [br]Relativistic effects are so strong that Seaborgium should lose its 6d electrons before its 7s electrons, which makes +6 its most stable state. It's [em3]predicted to be a body-centered cubic metal[em3] with a density of 23 to 24 g/cm³, though early estimates were as high as 35.[br] [br]Atoms are made one at a time, by [em1]firing ion beams at heavy targets[em1] or as decay products of heavier elements. Searches for long-lived Seaborgium in nature, such as in Tungsten ore, have all come up empty.[br] [br]Researchers at Berkeley and Livermore including Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg, and Kenneth Hulet [em3]discovered it in 1974[em3]. It's [em2]named for Glenn Seaborg[em2], who was [em1]still alive[em1] at the time. IUPAC objected at first, and the name was not formally adopted until August 1997. Only [link]Oganesson[link] has also been named for a then-living person.

name: Bohrium
info: [em3]Bohrium[em3] is the heavier relative of [link]Rhenium[link]. In 2000, chemists formed a [em2]volatile oxychloride from just six atoms[em2] of Bohrium. It was less volatile than Rhenium's, just as predicted, and its measured adsorption energy of 77.8 kJ/mol was within 1% of the calculated value.[br] [br]Calculations [em1]predict a hexagonal metal[em1] with a density of 26 to 27 g/cm³. Its +7 state should be easy to reach but unstable in water, where it would reduce to +4. A volatile heptoxide, Bh[sub]2[sub]O[sub]7[sub], is predicted that would dissolve in water to make [em3]'perbohric acid'[em3], HBhO[sub]4[sub].[br] [br][em1]Relativistic effects[em1] on its electrons, the same kind that give [link]Gold[link] its color and keep Mercury liquid, are expected to reverse some of the habits of lighter members of its group.[br] [br]In 1981 a team at GSI in Darmstadt, Germany, bombarded [link]Bismuth[link] with [link]Chromium[link] nuclei and [em3]made 5 atoms[em3] of [link]Bohrium-262[link]. The element is [em1]named after Danish physicist Niels Bohr[em1]. The German team proposed 'Nielsbohrium', but a committee recommended the shorter name.

name: Hassium
info: [em3]Hassium[em3] sits below [link]Osmium[link] in group 8 and behaves like it. Experiments confirmed that it [em2]reacts with Oxygen to form a volatile tetroxide[em2], HsO[sub]4[sub], and its adsorption was measured. Calculations predict a density of 27 to 29 g/cm³, which would beat Osmium, the [em1]densest element measured so far[em1], at 22.6.[br] [br][link]Hassium-270[link] is a candidate for a [em1]deformed doubly magic nucleus[em1], with 108 protons and 162 neutrons, a combination predicted to be especially stable. Theorists predict an [em3]island of stability[em3] for superheavy nuclei, though it may lie further away than first expected.[br] [br]In 1984 a team at the [em3]GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany[em3], led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg, made it by bombarding [link]Lead[link] with [link]Iron[link] nuclei. The [em1]name comes from Hassia[em1], the Latin name of Hesse, the German state where GSI is located. Only hundreds of atoms have ever been made, and it has no uses.

name: Meitnerium
info: [em3]Meitnerium[em3] is predicted to be among the [em2]densest of all elements[em2], at 27 to 28 g/cm³, with a face-centered cubic structure like [link]Iridium[link]. It's [em1]expected to be a noble metal[em1] like [link]Cobalt[link], [link]Rhodium[link], and Iridium, with +3 its most stable state in water and a volatile hexafluoride.[br] [br]Its [em1]chemistry has never been investigated[em1]. Chemistry needs at least four atoms, a half-life of at least one second, and about one atom produced per week. A 2002-2003 attempt at Berkeley detected no atoms, and when GSI tried subliming Rhodium compounds as stand-ins, they needed about 1000°C, far above the roughly 500°C limit of current methods.[br] [br]It's [em1]named for Lise Meitner[em1], an Austrian-Swedish physicist who helped discover nuclear fission and, with Otto Hahn, the element [link]Protactinium[link]. Meitnerium is the [em3]only element named solely for a non-mythical woman.[em3][br] [br]On August 29, 1982, a team at [em2]GSI in Darmstadt, Germany[em2], bombarded [link]Bismuth[link] with [link]Iron[link] nuclei and detected [em1]a single atom[em1] of [link]Meitnerium-266[link]. It has no uses.

name: Darmstadtium
info: [em3]Darmstadtium[em3] is predicted to be a body-centered cubic metal, unlike its group 10 relatives [link]Nickel[link], [link]Palladium[link], and [link]Platinum[link], with a density of 26 to 27 g/cm³, denser than [link]Osmium[link]. Like Platinum, it should form a [em1]volatile hexafluoride[em1], and +6 should be among its stable states.[br] [br]The most stable known isotope, [link]Darmstadtium-281[link], has a half-life of about 14 seconds and decays mostly by spontaneous fission. It's the only one long-lived enough for chemistry, but it can come only from the decay of [link]Flerovium-289[link]. A Japanese model predicts [em2]Darmstadtium-294[em2], with 184 neutrons, could last about 300 years.[br] [br]It was first detected on November 9, 1994, at [em1]GSI in Darmstadt, Germany[em1], under Sigurd Hofmann. His team fired [link]Nickel[link] ions at a [link]Lead[link] target and detected [em3]a single atom[em3] of [link]Darmstadtium-269[link]. It's [em2]named for the city where it was discovered[em2], and the team also considered 'Wixhausium', after a Darmstadt suburb. It has no uses beyond research.

name: Roentgenium
info: [em3]Roentgenium[em3] sits below [link]Gold[link] in group 11 and is predicted to be a [em2]noble metal[em2] like [link]Copper[link], [link]Silver[link], and Gold, but a body-centered cubic one with a density of 22 to 24 g/cm³, above [link]Osmium[link]'s. Its +3 state should be the most stable, with +5 also stable, and its first ionization energy should nearly match that of [link]Radon[link].[br] [br]Calculations also [em2]predict a stable cyanide complex[em2] like the one used to extract Gold, and a true heptafluoride, RgF[sub]7[sub], that decays at room temperature. Rg[sup]+[sup] ions should be the [em1]softest metal ions[em1] known, and negative roentgenide ions may not exist at all.[br] [br]On December 8, 1994, a team led by Sigurd Hofmann at [em1]GSI in Darmstadt, Germany[em1], bombarded [link]Bismuth[link] with [link]Nickel[link] nuclei and detected [em1]three atoms[em1] of Roentgenium-272. The element is [em3]named after Wilhelm Röntgen[em3], who discovered X-rays. Only a few atoms have ever been made, and they have no practical use.

name: Copernicium
info: [em3]Copernicium[em3] sits below [link]Mercury[link] in group 12, and calculations predict it's a [em2]liquid at room temperature[em2] that melts near 10°C and boils near 67°C, with a density of 14 g/cm³, close to Mercury's. Its first ionization energy nearly matches that of [link]Xenon[link], so it may [em3]act more like a noble gas[em3].[br] [br]Experiments in 2006 and 2007 with only five atoms on a Gold surface showed it's [em2]more volatile than Mercury[em2] and behaves like [link]Radon[link]. One estimate puts its boiling point at 84°C, give or take about 110.[br] [br][em1]Relativistic effects[em1] are predicted to be the largest of any group 12 element, so Copernicium ions may lose 6d electrons before 7s electrons, and CnF[sub]2[sub] may fall apart spontaneously.[br] [br]On 9 February 1996 a team at [em1]GSI in Darmstadt, Germany[em1], fired [link]Zinc[link] nuclei at a [link]Lead[link] target and produced [em1]a single atom[em1] of [link]Copernicium-277[link]. It's [em3]named for the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus[em3], and IUPAC accepted the name on 19 February 2010, his 537th birthday.

name: Nihonium
info: Discovered at the [em1]RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science[em1] in Japan, this element was officially named on November 28, 2016. The root of its name, [em3]Nihon[em3], is one of the two ways to say [em3]Japan[em3] in Japanese, literally meaning [em2]the Land of the Rising Sun[em2]. Nihonium is the first element to be discovered by an Asian country.

name: Flerovium
info: [em3]Flerovium[em3] is the [em2]heaviest known member of group 14[em2], below [link]Lead[link], and its chemistry is surprising. Early experiments found it [em1]unexpectedly volatile[em1], and newer results show it also acts like a metal, yet it may still be a gas at room temperature. It may melt near 11°C, with a density close to Lead's.[br] [br]Its inner electrons move so fast that [em3]relativity matters[em3]: a hydrogen-like Flerovium ion's electron would weigh about 1.79 times its resting mass, versus about 1.25 for Lead.[br] [br]Flerovium is predicted to lie near the center of the [em1]island of stability[em1]. Flerovium-298, with 184 neutrons, was long expected to be doubly magic, but no known pairing of beam and target can reach it.[br] [br]In December 1998 a team at the [em1]Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia[em1], led by Yuri Oganessian, bombarded [link]Plutonium[link] with [link]Calcium-48[link] nuclei and detected one atom. The [em3]name honors the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions[em3], named for physicist Georgy Flyorov, who in 1942 wrote to Joseph Stalin about the silence in Western nuclear fission research.

name: Moscovium
info: Officially named on November 28, 2016, [em3]Moscovium[em3] is so named in recognition of the [em3]Moscow[em3] region. This honors the ancient Russian land that is the home of the [em1]Joint Institute for Nuclear Research[em1] where the discovery experiments were conducted using the [em2]Dubna Gas-Filled Recoil Separator[em2] in combination with the heavy ion accelerator capabilities of the [em2]Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions[em2].

name: Livermorium
info: [em3]Livermorium[em3] is an extremely radioactive element that has never been observed in nature. As of 2020 only [em2]35 individual atoms[em2] of Livermorium have been created in laboratories.[br] [br]The first synthesis of Livermorium was in 2000 when scientists at the [em1]JINR lab in Dubna, Russia[em1] bombarded [link]Curium-248[link] with accelerated ions of [link]Calcium-48[link], producing a single atom via [em2]nuclear fusion[em2] which quickly decayed to [link]Flerovium-289[link].[br] [br]As a particularly large nucleus its inner shell electrons have an incredibly high velocity, approaching the [em3]speed of light[em3]. Due to its short half-life, little has been confirmed for how Livermorium would behave chemically, but being in the same group as [link]Oxygen[link] and [link]Sulfur[link] suggests it could form [em1]Livermorium Hydride (H[sub]2[sub]Lv)[em1], a similar compound to [em2]hydrogen sulfide (H[sub]2[sub]S) or water (H[sub]2[sub]O)[em2].

name: Tennessine
info: Officially named on November 28, 2016, [em3]Tennessine[em3] is so named in recognition of the contributions of the [em3]Tennessee[em3] region of the United States to superheavy element research. This region is home to the [em1]Oak Ridge National[em1] [em1]Laboratory[em1], [em1]Vanderbilt University[em1], and the [em1]University of Tennessee at Knoxville[em1].

name: Oganesson
info: Officially named on November 28, 2016, [em3]Oganesson[em3] honors [em2]Professor Yuri Oganessian[em2] for his pioneering contributions to research of superheavy elements. Among many achievements in the field he helped produce experimental evidence for the [em3]island of stability[em3].
